item.title: Quantum control of an electrically levitated nanoparticle with a trapped ion
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Parametric AC modulation of the ion-nanoparticle distance enables resonant Coulomb coupling across a frequency gap of Ωi′/Ωp′∼103, achieving sympathetic cooling of an electrically levitated nanoparticle to steady-state phonon occupation ⟨nˆp⟩≈0.1.

Grade 0.436 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “neutral atom tweezer arrays and Rydberg blockade entangling gates” · Bernard Faulend, Dmitry S. Bykov, Tracy E. Northup, Carlos Gonzalez-Ballestero

Figure

Steady-state nanoparticle phonon occupation ⟨nˆp⟩ss as a function of ion sideband cooling rate γi and coupling strength g′, demonstrating motional ground-state cooling below 1 phonon.

Asks

Can an electrically levitated nanoparticle co-trapped with a single ion in a linear Paul trap be resonantly coupled to the ion, cooled to its motional ground state, and driven into nonclassical states?

But

Theoretical model assuming laser phase feed-forward with Δfmax∼10 MHz, precooled radial modes below 30 mK, and an additional drive tone at 2ωd to suppress parametric instabilities.

Tools

linear Paul trap · Coulomb coupling modulation via AC endcap drive · continuous ion sideband cooling · laser phase feed-forward · master equation simulations

Abstract

Quantum control of levitated nanoparticles offers a route towards macroscopic quantum states. Here we propose a novel way to achieve it for a nanoparticle levitated electrically in a linear Paul trap together with a single ion, a system recently realized experimentally. By suitably engineering the trap's AC potential, one can parametrically modulate the ion-nanoparticle distance and thus the Coulomb coupling to enable a resonant interaction. For realistic parameters, we calculate that this enables sympathetic cooling of the nanoparticle to its motional ground state by a single, continuously laser-cooled ion. Additional AC drives enable the preparation of squeezed nanoparticle states and of ion-nanoparticle entanglement. Moreover, non-Gaussian states such as Fock and cat states, prepared in the ion with standard trapped-ion techniques, can be transferred to the nanoparticle with high fidelities. We provide complete protocols for each of these states, including all known decoherence sources. Our results establish electrically trapped ion-nanoparticle systems as a platform for quantum control of levitated matter.

item.title: 60-cm-long In-vacuum Zerodur Optical Cavity for Optical Lattice Atom Interferometry
item.description:
Worth a look new method — 60 cm-long in-vacuum Zerodur optical cavity achieves mirror vibration noise below 5 nm/Hz from 2 Hz to 100 kHz and resonance thermal drift of 15 MHz over 47 hours.

Grade 0.425 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Cavity-based quantum networks with single atoms and optical photons” · Philip Wondrak, Paola Luna, Kenneth Nakasone, Andrei Zhukov, Michael Grisham, Garrett D. Cole, Po-han Chen, Cristian D. Panda

Asks

Can an in-vacuum optical cavity provide the optical access, thermal stability, and vibration suppression required for 1 mm wavepacket separation and 1-minute coherence in optical lattice atom interferometers?

But

Cavity characterized empty under ultrahigh-vacuum conditions; atom interferometry coherence times and spatial separations are projected targets.

Tools

Zerodur cavity spacer · integrated differential pumping · piezoelectric cavity stabilization · in-situ optical interferometry vibration monitoring

Abstract

Optical cavities are widely used in atomic physics experiments to control the spatial geometry and spectral properties of atom-light interactions. Recently, an optical lattice generated by the pristine mode of an optical cavity was utilized to hold and extend the quantum coherence of atomic spatial superpositions. Here, we describe an in-vacuum optical cavity designed to enhance the spatial and temporal coherence of optical lattice atom interferometers to one millimeter wavepacket separations and one minute measurement durations. The cavity uses a rigid Zerodur spacer to suppress the negative effects of thermal drift and mechanical-acoustic vibrations on the atomic motional state. The 60 cm-long cavity spacer provides ample optical access for the laser beams and imaging optics necessary for the preparation, quantum control, and read-out of the atomic state, as well as room for various source mass configurations for localized gravitational measurements. An integrated differential pumping structure enables compatibility with ultrahigh-vacuum operation and optical interferometry allows for in-situ vibration monitoring. The performance of the optical cavity is methodically characterized: we measure mirror vibration noise with amplitude below 5 nm/√Hz in a wide frequency range of 2 Hz - 100 kHz and a slow 15 MHz thermal drift of the cavity resonance over 47 hours, which can be readily stabilized with an integrated piezo. The optical cavity supports both 852-nm light for Raman transitions and 1064-nm light for the optical lattice, with a free spectral range matched to an integer divisor of the cesium ground-state hyperfine splitting.

item.title: Frequency-bin-encoded quantum secret sharing with fast basis switching
item.description:
Long shot new result — Demonstrated three-party quantum secret sharing encoded entirely in frequency bins with active electrical basis and state switching at 20 MHz symbol rates. Maintained three-party correlations ≥0.9105(78) with quantum bit error rates ≤4.47(39)%.

Grade 0.416 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Cavity-based quantum networks with single atoms and optical photons” · Chen-You Su, Suparna Seshadri, Hsuan-Hao Lu, Jason D. McKinney, Andrew M. Weiner, Joseph M. Lukens

Figure

Three-party correlation parameter ⟨ϵs⟩ (vertical axis) measured under active pseudorandom switching at 20 MHz across 16 state-and-basis combinations (horizontal axis), grouped by Alice-Bob basis and Sara's state.

Asks

Can active fast state preparation and basis switching be achieved in multiparty quantum communication encoded in frequency bins?

Before

Liquid-crystal-on-silicon pulse shapers for frequency-bin state control operated with ms-scale switching times.

But

Co-located setup sharing a common RF source over ∼10 m-scale fibers. Central 45 ns of each 50 ns interval retained (temporal windowing guard band of 2.5 ns, ∼0.5 dB loss). Evaluated with pseudorandom rather than true quantum random sequences.

Tools

analog RF phase shifters · electro-optic phase modulators · PPLN waveguide entangled-pair source · superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors (SNSPDs)

Abstract

Frequency-bin encoding offers unique opportunities for fiber-native quantum information processing, yet its full potential has been hampered by challenges in rapid state control and protocol scaling. Leveraging high-speed microwave processing, we overcome several extant hurdles and unlock new fundamental capabilities in frequency-based quantum communications. First, we demonstrate three-party quantum secret sharing, representing, to our knowledge, the first multiparty (N≥3 users) quantum communication protocol implemented entirely with frequency encoding. Second, we demonstrate active, pseudorandom switching of frequency-bin quantum states and measurement bases at 20 MHz symbol rates, enabling real-time protocol operation without relying on hardware-intensive passive basis-selection schemes. Even under fast switching, we preserve high-contrast three-party correlations (≥0.91) and low quantum bit error rates (≤4.5%). Our work extends frequency-bin quantum communication beyond static, two-party protocols, opening a pathway toward scalable, reconfigurable, and real-time spectrally encoded quantum networking.
